analytic.title: Resource-Aware Partitioned Scheduling for Heterogeneous Multicore Real-Time Systems

div.p: Heterogeneous multicore processors have become popular computing engines for modern embedded real-time systems recently. However, there is rather limited research on the scheduling of real-time tasks running on heterogeneous multicore systems with shared resources. Note that, different partitionings of tasks upon heterogeneous cores can affect the synchronization overheads of tasks (and thus the system schedulability). Focusing on the partitioned-EDF scheduling and resource access protocol MSRP (Multiprocessor Stack Resource Policy), this paper proposes an effective synchronization aware task partitioning algorithm for heterogeneous multicores (SA-TPA-HM). Several resource-oriented heuristics are exploited to tighten the bound on the synchronization costs of tasks through dynamic task prioritization and to find an appropriate core for each task that can minimize the system utilization increment. The simulation results show that our proposed SA-TPA-HM scheme can achieve higher acceptance ratio (e.g., 60% more), when compared to the existing schemes designed for homogeneous multicores.

div.head: INTRODUCTION
div.p: With the goal of satisfying application performance while maintaining power efficiency of computing systems, heterogeneous multicore processors (such as Intel ąŕs QuickIA platform [4] and ARM big.LITTLE [15]) have emerged as popular computing engines for diverse embedded real-time applications, e.g., consumer multimedia [8] and video object tracking [10]. For tasks co-running on multicore systems, they may need to access shared resources (e.g., shared data objects) exclusively and such resource access contention can lead to the problem of task synchronization. For real-time applications, the task synchronization problem becomes more salient as Permission to make digital or hard copies of all or part of this work for personal or classroom use is granted without fee provided that copies are not made or distributed for profit or commercial advantage and that copies bear this notice and the full citation on the first page. The priority inversion stemmed from the resource access race can delay the execution of high-priority tasks and thus may result in degraded schedulability of tasks.

To address the problem of task synchronization, several lock based resource access protocols have been investigated. For uniprocessors, Sha et al. developed a Priority Ceiling Protocol (PCP) [14] for fixed priority scheduling and Baker proposed a Stack Resource Policy (SRP) [1] for dynamic priority scheduling. Based on the principle of these protocols for uniprocessors, MSRP [5], MPCP [11] and several protocols [2,3] have been extended and explored for multiprocessors. Moreover, several studies on the resource-aware real-time scheduling have been reported in [6,7,17]. Although the real-time scheduling for heterogeneous multicores has been studied [12,16], there is very rare work on the scheduling of real-time tasks that access shared resources in heterogeneous multicore systems.

It is noteworthy that improper mappings of tasks on heterogeneous cores can cause larger synchronization overheads of tasks and inflated system utilization, which can degrade the system schedulability significantly. In this work, for periodic real-time tasks that access shared resources, by incorporating several resource-oriented heuristics, we study a synchronization-aware task partitioning algorithm for heterogeneous multicores (SA-TPA-HM). We adopt the resource access protocol MSRP [5] since it has simpler implementation and better schedulability performance than other protocols (such as MPCP [11]). Specifically, with the reduced synchronization costs of tasks, SA-TPA-HM exploits a dynamic priority method to order those unmapped tasks by computing their maximum estimated task utilizations in an iterative manner. We further study an effective task allocation heuristic for better schedulability, where each task is assigned onto the core that leads to the minimum system utilization increment under partitioned-EDF and MSRP.

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. Section 2 presents system models and necessary preliminaries about resource access protocol MSRP. In Section 3, the task mapping algorithm SA-TPA-HM is proposed. Simulation results are given and discussed in Section 4. Section 5 concludes the paper.

div.head: SYSTEM MODELS AND PRELIMINARIES
div.p: We consider a heterogeneous multicore system that consists of M processor cores ({P 1 , . . . , P M }) with different execution frequencies (speeds) [12,16], where the speed of processor core P i is denoted as f i . For ease of presentations, we assume that the processor core with smaller index has slower speed (i.e.,
div.formula: f 1 ≤ f 2 ≤ . . . ≤ f M ) and f 1 is normalized to 1.
div.p: A set of N periodic real-time tasks Ψ = {τ 1 , . . . ,τ N } run on the system with their initial arrivals at time 0. Every task τ i has a period (i.e., relative deadline) p i . That is, the j t h job of task τ i arrives at time (j -1) • p i and has to finish by its absolute deadline j • p i . The worst-case execution time (WCET) of task τ i based on the lowest speed of cores (i.e., 1) is denoted as c i . Then, the WCET of task
div.formula: τ i on core P m is c i f m
div.p: . With the focus on the partitioned scheduling, the EDF scheduler is deployed on each core P m (m = 1, • • • ,M) and schedules all its tasks in the subset Ψ m . Then, we have Ψ = ∪ M m=1 Ψ m . As there is at most one active job for any real-time task at any time, we use task and job exchangeably in the remainder of this paper without specified otherwise.

This work considers shared data (e.g., global variables) among tasks, instead of hardware resources (such as bus, cache and network) that can be handled by their corresponding schemes [9,18]. With shared resources being considered, the system is assumed to have a set of R resources R = {R 1 , . . . , R R } that can be shared by all tasks without deploying dedicated cores for resources. The access to any resource by a task is exclusive and non-preemptable, i.e., a resource can be held and accessed by only one task at any time. Moreover, we focus on non-nested critical sections as the nested ones occur rarely in practice and can be tackled by group locks [2]. There are n i critical sections in task τ i and its x th critical section is denoted as z i,x , where task τ i accesses resource r i,x (∈ R) for the maximum time c i,x based on the lowest speed of cores.

div.head: Resource Access Protocol MSRP
div.p: We first briefly review the principles of MSRP [5] where its basic rules can be summarized as follows:

• When a task τ i on core P m (i.e., τ i ∈ Ψ m ) issues a request for a resource R a , if resource R a is free, task τ i locks and then accesses it non-preemptively; otherwise, if resource R a is currently held and accessed by another task from different core, task τ i is appended to the FIFO queue of resource R a and the core P m enters a busy-waiting status; • Once task τ i completes accessing resource R a , it unlocks resource R a and becomes preemptable again. If resource R a 's FIFO queue is not empty (i.e., there exist tasks on other cores waiting for accessing resource R a ), its header task is de-queued and then locks the resource.
From the above rules of MSRP, we can see that the execution of a task τ i on core P m can be blocked due to resource access contention at two different scenarios as follows:

• When task τ i requests access to a resource R a that is currently accessed by a task from another core, it has to wait in the FIFO queue of R a and such duration caused by intercore synchronization interference is denoted as global waiting time (or busy-waiting time); • When a low-priority task on core P m is busy-waiting for or holding a resource, task τ i is locally blocked and such duration is denoted as local blocking time.

For periodic tasks that access shared resources (protected within their non-nested critical sections) and are scheduled by EDF and MSRP, we can have the following properties [5]: PROPERTY 1. For any core at any given time, there exists at most one task that is either holding a resource or busy-waiting for a resource that is currently held by a task on different core. PROPERTY 2. Any job of a task can be blocked by a low-priority job on the same core at most once. PROPERTY 3. A job's local blocking time is bounded by the longest duration of any low-priority job on the same core that busywaits for (if applicable) and accesses a resource once.

Problem Description: for a set Ψ of periodic real-time tasks that access shared resources in a heterogeneous multicore system, find a feasible task-to-core mapping Π where tasks on every core are schedulable under EDF and MSRP. Clearly, when the system is homogeneous without shared resources, the problem actually reduces to the classical bin-packing problem, which is known to be NP-hard in the strong sense. Hence, the partition problem considered in this work is NP-hard as well.

div.head: PARTITIONING ALGORITHM SA-TPA-HM
div.p: For partitioned scheduling, there are generally two essential phases when designating tasks to cores: a) determine the order of tasks to be allocated; and b) find appropriate cores to accommodate tasks. Considering the varying synchronization overheads of tasks for different mappings of tasks on heterogeneous cores, we propose a synchronization-aware task partitioning algorithm for heterogeneous multicores (SA-TPA-HM) to improve tasks' schedulability.

div.head: Overview of SA-TPA-HM
div.p: The outline of SA-TPA-HM is summarized in Algorithm 1. First, the corresponding parameters are initialized in line 1. For all unmapped tasks in the set Γ, we select the highest-priority task one at a time, where the priorities of unmapped tasks are updated subject to their iteratively estimated utilizations (line 3). Then, the target core is chosen based on the system utilization increment for M possible task allocations (line 4). If the current partial mapping is feasible, the utilizations of all cores are updated accordingly (line 8). Finally, SA-TPA-HM either fails or returns the feasible partition Π (line 11). We present the detailed heuristics in what follows.

div.head: Reduced Waiting Times for Allocated Tasks
div.p: For a task τ i , different from the rather pessimistic approach to calculating its total global waiting time by simply accumulating BW i,x (see (1)) as in [5,6], SA-TPA-HM intends to reduce the maximum busy-waiting times and maximum estimated ones for allocated tasks and un-mapped tasks respectively in a resource-oriented way. Recall that the initial arrival time of any task is 0. We first analyze the limits on inter-core synchronization interference (due to accessing the same resource) for tasks on different cores. Such inter-core interference among tasks can be presented as follows [7].

div.head: Utilization Estimates of Unmapped Tasks
div.p: It is well-known that the partitions generated by the utilization decreasing policy can achieve better schedulability [13]. Based on the feasibility condition for MSRP as presented in Proposition 2.1, we see that for each task, in addition to its WCET, its global waiting time and local blocking time can also affect the core utilization. Intuitively, the global waiting time plays a more important role in the core utilization compared to local blocking time based on their definitions. Then, following the principle of utilization deceasing policy, the estimated utilization for an unmapped task τ i can be defined as u est i = (c i + BW est i )/p i , where BW est i is the estimated total busy-waiting time for task τ i to access all its resources.

For unmapped task τ i , we try to compute the worst-case BW est i , where task τ i is assumed to be assigned to the fasted core (i.e., P M ) and can experience the worst-case global waiting caused by the tasks from other slower cores (i.e., P 1 , . . . , P M -1 ). As the global waiting time of a task relies on a specific task-to-core partition, getting minimum BW est i of unmapped task τ i has the same time complexity as the partitioned problem. To reduce BW est i with acceptable time complexity, we first obtain the set of critical sections C i,a , which can cause the worst-case inter-core interference on each resource R a (∈ Φ i ) that task τ i needs to access. Here, a critical section may appear multiple times in the set C i,a . The basic steps to obtain the set C i,,a are shown in Algorithm 3.

Similar to Algorithm 2, Algorithm 3 relies on the current mapping Π and inter-core interference limits. Specifically, an additional total remaining limit (i.e., total) is employed since the number of inter-core interference on task τ i when it accesses resource R a is at most (M -1) • |S i,a | based on Property 1. First, the remaining limits on the number of interference from slower cores (i.e., P 1 , . . . , P M -1 ) and the set C i,a are initialized (line 1). Algorithm 3 omits the critical sections of tasks that have been allocated to core P M (line 4), and handles the interference limits from mapped tasks (line 6) and unmapped ones (line 8) differently. Here, for the critical section in un-allocated task τ j whose exact assignment is unknown till now, the number of its interference on task τ i complies with the limits from π i,j , |S i,a | and total. Moreover, for those critical sections considered, they are added to the set C i,a individually subject to the interference limits (lines 10 to 12). As the critical sections in the set S i a are sorted by their non-ascending sizes, the critical sections in the set C i,a can be obtained by the same order. When there exists no remaining interference (line 13) or all critical sections in the set S i a have been tested, the resulting C i,a is returned. Again, to find the estimated busy-waiting time of task τ i in the worst case, the task with larger critical sections in C i,a needs to be allocated to a slower core subject to its interference limits. Based on C i,a obtained by Algorithm 3, the detailed steps to compute BW est i, R a for un-allocated task τ i to access its resource R a are shown in Algorithm 4. Algorithm 4 is comprised of two basic steps: step one computes the estimated global waiting time BW est i, R a caused by tasks that are already allocated (lines 2 to 6); second step calculates BW est i, R a contributed by unmapped tasks (lines 7 to 15). Based on the inter-core interference limit, if there is no interference from a core, the remaining critical sections in the set C i,a are processed on the next faster core (line 8). Once all critical sections in the set C i,a have been processed, the resulting BW est i, R a is returned (line 12). div.head: Selection of Target Core
div.p: The second phase of partitioned scheduling is the selection of a core for a given task. To find an appropriate core to accommodate the candidate task τ i , we study an effective heuristic for better schedulability of the task system, where every task allocation should lead to the minimized increase in the system utilization.

Based on (3), we define the new utilization of core P m with a new task τ i as U (Ψ m ∪ {τ i }). If U (Ψ m ∪ {τ i }) > 1, task τ i does not fit on core P m and there is U (Ψ m ∪ {τ i }) = ∞. Note that, after task τ i is mapped to a core P m , the utilizations of other cores may change by this new task due to task synchronization. Then, for another core P x , the synchronization overheads of all its tasks need to be updated accordingly and its new core utilization is denoted as
div.formula: U τ i (Ψ x ). Similarly, U τ i (Ψ x ) = ∞ if U τ i (Ψ x ) > 1.
div.p: Therefore, the new system utilization with task τ i on core P m is defined as:
div.formula: U (Π ∪ {τ i }) = max{U (Ψ m ∪ {τ i }), max{U τ i (Ψ x )| (4) ∀x : x m}}.
div.p: Based on the feasibility condition as shown in Proposition 2.1, assuming that τ i is allocated to core P m , the system utilization increment for this mapping is defined as ∆ sys τ i , P m = U (Π∪{τ i }) -U (Π). By probing M possible assignments for task τ i and updating the new utilizations for all cores based on (4), the core P k that results in valid minimum system utilization increment (i.e., ∆ sys τ i , P k ≤ 1) is chosen. If there is no feasible core for task τ i , SA-TPA-HM fails and returns null. When there exists more than one such core, the tie-breaking prefers the core with larger index (i.e., the faster core).

div.head: EVALUATIONS AND DISCUSSIONS
div.p: In this section, we evaluate the performance of the proposed SA-TPA-HM through extensive simulations. For comparison, we extended the existing synchronization-aware WFD (SA-WFD) by taking the different speeds of cores into account [6]. To assess the effectiveness of the task ordering policy exploited by SA-TPA-HM (see Section 3.3), we also implemented SA-TPA-HM without task ordering (SA-TPA-HM-WTO), where those unmapped tasks are sorted by their non-increasing raw task utilizations (i.e., c i p i for each task τ i ). We compare these mapping schemes based on the performance metric: schedulability ratio, which is defined as the ratio of the number of task sets having feasible partitions under these schemes over the total number of tested task sets generated as follows.

For the results reported below, each data point corresponds to the average of 30, 000 task sets. Generally, a larger N SRU represents higher system workload. SA-TPA-HM considers the influence of the system heterogeneity and synchronization costs of tasks on the feasibility. Moreover, it tries to minimize the system utilization increment for each task allocation. Thus, SA-TPA-HM has the highest acceptance ratio, especially for higher system workload (e.g., N SRU ≥ 0.7). As SA-TPA-HM uses a dynamic task ordering policy, it can obtain better performance compared to SA-TPA-HM-WTO. Moreover, SA-TPA-HM-WTO outperforms SA-WFD, which focuses on the similarity of tasks accessing the same resources in homogeneous multicores while employing the pessimistic global waiting times for (unmapped and allocated) tasks and neglecting the effects of system heterogeneity on their synchronization overheads (thus the system utilization) during task-to-core mappings. larger CSR indicates higher resource access contention among tasks with other parameters being fixed. As can be seen from Figure 1(b), when CSR becomes larger, the acceptance ratio of SA-WFD drops quickly; in contrast, SA-TPA-HM exhibits relatively steady performance due to its resource-guided heuristics for heterogeneous systems as discussed in Section 3. Similarly, compared to SA-TPA-HM-WTO, SA-TPA-HM can achieve higher acceptance ratio thanks to its iterative prioritization approach for un-assigned tasks to increase the schedulability of the task system.

div.head: Simulation Results
div.p: Figure 1(c) depicts the performance of the mapping schemes when the number of resources R varies. Intuitively, smaller R implies more synchronization requirements in the system when other parameters are fixed. Similar to the trends as shown in Figure 1(b), when R becomes smaller, SA-TPA-HM and SA-TPA-HM-WTO can have much better schedulability performance compared to SA-WFD based on the above-mentioned reasons.

Figure 1(d) further illustrates the performance comparison with varying number of cores M (where N = 4 • M). When other parameters are fixed, more cores often means more inter-core synchronization interference among tasks. For this case (e.g., M = 16), SA-TPA-HM and SA-TPA-HM-WTO can obtain much higher acceptance ratio (e.g., 60% more) compared to SA-WFD.

div.head: CONCLUSIONS
div.p: For periodic real-time tasks executing on heterogeneous multicore systems with shared resources that are scheduled by partitioned-EDF and MSRP, we first study a resource-guided approach to tightening the bound on the synchronization overheads of tasks. With the different speeds of cores and synchronization costs of tasks being considered, the proposed SA-TPA-HM uses an iterative ordering scheme to prioritize unmapped tasks based on their maximum estimated utilizations. SA-TPA-HM further guarantees that each task mapping can minimize the increment in system utilization. Finally, the simulation results confirm the effectiveness of SA-TPA-HM.

figure.figDesc: Figure 1(a) shows the impacts of different N SRU on the performance of the mapping schemes. To clearly exhibit the performance comparison among the schemes, N SRU is chosen within [0.4, 0.75].Generally, a larger N SRU represents higher system workload. SA-TPA-HM considers the influence of the system heterogeneity and synchronization costs of tasks on the feasibility. Moreover, it tries to minimize the system utilization increment for each task allocation. Thus, SA-TPA-HM has the highest acceptance ratio, especially for higher system workload (e.g., N SRU ≥ 0.7). As SA-TPA-HM uses a dynamic task ordering policy, it can obtain better performance compared to SA-TPA-HM-WTO. Moreover, SA-TPA-HM-WTO outperforms SA-WFD, which focuses on the similarity of tasks accessing the same resources in homogeneous multicores while employing the pessimistic global waiting times for (unmapped and allocated) tasks and neglecting the effects of system heterogeneity on their synchronization overheads (thus the system utilization) during task-to-core mappings.
